## Web app libraries

- Render components with `h(component, props, ...children)`. Do not call component functions directly (e.g. `h(button, { label })`, not `button({ label })`). This lets React invoke components and preserves hook behavior. `h` is from `lib/web/hyperscript.ts` and is installed globally by the web prelude.
- `h(tag, props?, ...children)` also accepts DOM tags. String tags can include classes, e.g. `h('div.panel', props, child)`.
- `use_state`, `use_ref`, `use_effect`, and `use_mount` from `lib/web/react.ts` are project hook wrappers. `use_state` returns `[value, set_value]`; calling the setter with no argument toggles a boolean. Effects can return cleanup functions.
- `s(initial_value, options)` from `lib/web/state.ts` declares shared state and returns a hook. Options used in this app include `localstorage` and `url_param`; `init_localstorage_prefix(name)` scopes persisted keys.
- `use_keyboard(key, handler, options)` from `lib/web/use keyboard.ts` registers a shortcut; use `when` for conditional activation.
- `use_sync_theme` and `use_window_active` are hooks from `lib/web/use sync theme.ts` and `lib/web/use window active.ts`.
- The web prelude `lib/web/global.ts` installs React, web helpers, and shared utilities as globals. For an unfamiliar unimported name, check the prelude and its defining module; don't assume it is a React built-in.
- tsconfig path starts from source, not source/web

content.text:
There’s **no deliberate multi-second delay** in the active generation path that I found.

In `web/component/app.ts`, sending a prompt awaits `init` if needed, then `send`, then `generate`. On the backend, `backend/actions.ts` starts generation immediately; `backend/generation.ts` prepares the conversation context, broadcasts the empty assistant message, resolves the endpoint/model/key, logs the request, and calls `utility/generate.ts`. That function starts a timer immediately before `fetch()` and reads the response stream as it arrives.

The main code-side work before the upstream request is context construction and configuration/key resolution. I don’t see a sleep, retry loop, or buffering-until-complete in that path. Streamed content/reasoning is appended as soon as it’s parsed.

So if you’re seeing several seconds before the first token, **the endpoint/model is the leading suspect**, though the app’s request/network path and the server’s context/config preparation can contribute. There’s no timing breakdown for those stages yet: the recorded `time_to_first_token` in `utility/generate.ts` is measured from just before `fetch()` to the first nonempty content or reasoning delta, so it includes upstream latency, network transit, and local stream parsing—not the UI’s earlier `init`/`send` steps. Also, it measures the first *text/reasoning* delta, not necessarily the endpoint’s first SSE event.

queries.answer:
## The Latency & DX Optimization Cookbook

When building interactive developer tools, coding agents, or low-latency conversational apps, total perceived latency is governed by two separate phases:

- Time to First Token (TTFT): Network transit + provider queue wait time + prompt prefill.
- Streaming time: The time from the first token to the last, set by the provider’s decode speed.

OpenRouter’s throughput (TPS) metric includes time to first token. For an individual request, it is output tokens divided by the time from sending the request to the provider until the response ends. Holding decode speed and other conditions constant, a slow first token lowers TPS, and shorter outputs have lower per-request TPS. Model pages, `sort: "throughput"`, and `preferred_min_throughput` use aggregated throughput statistics from eligible completions; very short completions are excluded from those aggregates. The formula below describes an individual request, not a latency prediction obtained by dividing your output length by a displayed provider percentile.

```
TPS ≈ Output Tokens / (TTFT + Streaming Time)
Total Latency ≈ TTFT + Streaming Time ≈ Output Tokens / TPS

```

Below are drop-in request configurations for common developer experience (DX) optimization scenarios. See the provider routing guide for the full API reference on `sort`, `partition`, `preferred_max_latency`, and `preferred_min_throughput`.

### Recipe 1: Bounding Peak-Hour Queue Latency

Scenario: During peak global traffic hours (e.g. US morning rush), popular open-weight inference hosts can experience queue congestion, causing Time to First Token (TTFT) to spike. Solution: Use `preferred_max_latency` with a percentile cutoff (such as `p90`).

...

- Rolling 5-Minute Window: Evaluates performance over the last 5 minutes, rapidly adapting when a host starts queueing.
- Soft Reordering (Zero 404 Risk): Providers that meet the threshold are promoted to the front of the candidate list.
Source: Latency and Performance | Minimizing Gateway Latency (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/latency-and-performance)

OpenRouter routes requests to the best available providers for your model. By default, OpenRouter routes each request based on each provider’s measured price, throughput, latency, and reliability. You can customize how your requests are routed using the `provider` object in the request body for the Responses API and Chat Completions.

...

| `sort` | string | object | - | Sort providers by price,

...

| `preferred_max_latency` | number | object | - | Preferred maximum latency (seconds). Can be a number or an object with percentile cutoffs (p50, p75, p90, p99).

...

## Default Routing

For each model in your request, OpenRouter picks a provider by comparing what a good response would actually cost you at each one, not by list price alone. Each input is measured from recent production traffic, so routing reacts within minutes when a provider gets faster, slower, or less reliable:

- Effective price: the price the provider actually charges, reflecting its real cache hit rate and its typical mix of input and output tokens.
- Throughput: end-to-end output tokens per second. A faster provider can charge more and still win your request.
- Time to first token (TTFT): how long you wait before the response starts streaming.
- Rate limits: how often the provider rejects requests with a 429 because it is out of capacity.
- Reliability: how often requests fail because of the provider.
- Quality: whether the provider’s tool calls come back well formed.

Providers close to the best share most of the traffic, and each request picks one at random, weighted by those shares. Providers far behind still get a small share, so routing notices when they improve. On top of the shares:

- A provider whose errors or 429s are far worse than the model’s other providers gets no traffic until it recovers.
- Routing learns how much load each provider can take before it returns 429s, and sends the rest to other providers.
- A burst of 429s or a jump in latency briefly lowers a provider’s share.

If a request fails, the retry is picked the same way from the providers that are left. Follow-up requests in a conversation stay with the same provider while its prompt cache is warm. For more detail on each input, see How OpenRouter Routes Traffic Between Providers.

When you send a request with `tools` or `tool_choice`, OpenRouter makes a best effort to route to providers known to support tool use. Similarly, if you set `max_output_tokens` (or `max_tokens` on Chat Completions), then OpenRouter will only route to providers that support a response of that length.

Default routing applies whenever you leave the choice of provider to OpenRouter. It is bypassed when you set `sort` (or a default provider sort in your account settings), use the `:floor` or `:nitro` shortcuts, set `order`, or use your own provider key. If you set `only` or `ignore` and two or more providers remain, default routing picks among them.

## Provider Sorting

As described above, default routing balances price against throughput, latency, and reliability. If you instead want to explicitly prioritize a particular provider attribute, you can include the `sort` field in the `provider` preferences. Default routing is bypassed, and the router will try providers in that order. The three sort options are:

- `"price"`: prioritize lowest price
- `"throughput"`: prioritize highest throughput
- `"latency"`: prioritize lowest latency

...

## Performance Thresholds

You can set minimum throughput or maximum latency thresholds to filter endpoints. Endpoints that don’t meet these thresholds are deprioritized (moved to the end of the list) rather than excluded entirely.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `preferred_min_throughput` | number | object | - | Preferred minimum throughput in tokens per second. Can be a number (applies to p50) or an object with percentile cutoffs. |
| `preferred_max_latency` | number | object | - | Preferred maximum latency in seconds. Can be a number (applies to p50) or an object with percentile cutoffs. |

### How Percentiles Work

OpenRouter tracks latency and throughput metrics for each model and provider using percentile statistics calculated over a rolling 5-minute window. The available percentiles are:

- p50 (median): 50% of requests perform better than this value
- p75: 75% of requests perform better than this value
- p90: 90% of requests perform better than this value
- p99: 99% of requests perform better than this value

Higher percentiles (like p90 or p99) give you more confidence about worst-case performance, while lower percentiles (like p50) reflect typical performance. For example, if a model and provider has a p90 latency of 2 seconds, that means 90% of requests complete in under 2 seconds. When you specify multiple percentile cutoffs, all specified cutoffs must be met for a model and provider to be in the preferred group. This allows you to set both typical and worst-case performance requirements.
Source: Provider Routing - Smart Multi-Provider Request Management (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection)

### Speed

Speed is the main factor that trades off against price: a faster endpoint can cost more and still win traffic. It’s measured as output tokens per second, end to end, so it includes TTFT: the user waits for the whole response, from sending the request to the last token.

### TTFT

TTFT adds directly to your adjusted price, even though it already counts toward speed, because interactive use depends on it most. It’s the time to first token: how long users wait before your response starts streaming. In agentic sessions, a model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.
Source: How OpenRouter Routes Traffic Between Providers (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/providers/traffic-routing)

## What one try costs: price plus waiting

For each request, the router estimates how many input and output tokens it will use from the model’s recent traffic. That one estimate sets both parts of a try: the price you would pay and the time you would wait.

### Effective price

Effective price is the price that the provider would actually charge you, calculated from recent measured traffic. It reflects the provider’s real cache hit rate and the model’s average mix of input and output tokens, so it can differ a lot from the list price. This ensures that a provider can’t win traffic by hiding expensive cached or output tokens behind a low input price.

The router prices your request at each provider’s effective price, and prioritizes the cheapest options.

### Throughput

Throughput is what trades off against price: a faster provider can charge more and still win your request. It’s measured as output tokens per second end-to-end, so it includes the time to first token plus the time it takes the provider to stream the entire output response. The router adds that wait to the Routing Cost using a conversion rate set per model, based on what its providers typically charge and how fast they are.

### Time to first token

Time to first token (TTFT) is how long you would wait before the response started streaming. It adds to the Routing Cost on its own, even though it already counts toward throughput, because interactive use depends on it most. In an agent session, the model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.

...

In order to measure the impact of the new routing algorithm, we had to go beyond a standard A/B test, because changes in routing behavior can’t easily be isolated from the control group. For example, if the new algorithm did a better job of routing traffic away from a struggling provider, the old algorithm’s requests to that provider would find more capacity available and get faster, skewing the results. Further compounding the difficulty is the enormous variability in request shape and volume patterns. A single whale user that spins up an automated flurry of high effort requests to a single provider can artificially inflate the metrics for that provider regardless of which algorithm we used to route their requests.

So we ran a switchback experiment: We split each day into 3-hour blocks and flipped each matched pair of blocks between the new and old router, with a one-hour burn-in period of discarded data each changeover, and measured the per-model impact across a representative sample of open source models over one full week.

## Results

Over the week of the experiment, we split over 24 million requests with 103 billion input tokens evenly between the old and new routing algorithms, measuring the impact on key performance metrics.

| Measure | Legacy | New Algorithm | New vs legacy | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TTFT p50 | 1,007 ms | 837 ms | 16.9% lower | 13.9% to 19.8% lower |
| TTFT p95 | 4,601 ms | 3,733 ms | 18.9% lower | 15.7% to 21.9% lower |
| Throughput p50 | 62.4 tok/s | 72.6 tok/s | 16.3% higher | 13.8% to 18.9% higher |
| Cost per K requests | $1.25 | $1.32 | 6.0% higher | 5.1% to 7.0% higher |
| Cost per M tokens | $0.301 | $0.324 | 7.3% higher | 4.9% to 9.6% higher |
| Caller TTFT p50 | 1,130 ms | 941 ms | 16.7% lower | 13.8% to 19.7% lower |
| Caller TTFT p95 | 6,032 ms | 4,504 ms | 25.3% lower | 21.6% to 29.0% lower |
| Whole request p50 (time to last token) | 4.00 s | 3.24 s | 19.0% lower | 14.2% to 23.6% lower |
| Whole request p95 | 41.5 s | 34.9 s | 16.0% lower | 12.2% to 19.7% lower |
| Hit at least one 429 | 7.1% | 3.8% | −3.3 pt 46% fewer | -2.5 to −4.2 pt 35% to 59% fewer |
| Needed a retry | 10.4% | 6.9% | −3.5 pt 34% fewer | -2.6 to -4.4 pt 25% to 42% fewer |
| Time spent in failed attempts, per req | 349 ms | 242 ms | −106 ms 30% less | -35 to −181 ms 10% to 52% less |
Source: How OpenRouter rebuilt provider routing for better, faster inference (https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/how-we-rebuilt-provider-routing/)
Published: 2026-10-28 | Authors: Scott Morse

| Metric | What it measures | When it matters | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Latency (time to first token) | The time between sending a request and receiving the first generated token | User-facing chat, agents, streaming interfaces, and interactive workflows | p90 and p99 latency, not only typical latency |

...

A provider can look fast at the start of a response and still feel slow by the time the full answer finishes. Time to first token (TTFT) captures the first part of that experience. Throughput covers the whole response: OpenRouter divides output tokens by the time from sending the request to the provider until the last token, so a slow first token also lowers throughput, and short replies score lower than long ones from the same provider. A provider with strong TTFT can still produce a weak long-form experience if its sustained token rate drops, while a provider with strong throughput can still feel poor in a chat interface if the first token arrives late.
Source: How to Evaluate LLM Provider Performance (https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/evaluate-llm-provider-performance/)

## The Latency & DX Optimization Cookbook

When building interactive developer tools, coding agents, or low-latency conversational apps, total perceived latency is governed by two separate phases:

- Time to First Token (TTFT): Network transit + provider queue wait time + prompt prefill.
- Streaming time: The time from the first token to the last, set by the provider’s decode speed.

OpenRouter’s throughput (TPS) metric includes time to first token. For an individual request, it is output tokens divided by the time from sending the request to the provider until the response ends. Holding decode speed and other conditions constant, a slow first token lowers TPS, and shorter outputs have lower per-request TPS. Model pages, `sort: "throughput"`, and `preferred_min_throughput` use aggregated throughput statistics from eligible completions; very short completions are excluded from those aggregates. The formula below describes an individual request, not a latency prediction obtained by dividing your output length by a displayed provider percentile.

```
TPS ≈ Output Tokens / (TTFT + Streaming Time)
Total Latency ≈ TTFT + Streaming Time ≈ Output Tokens / TPS

```

Below are drop-in request configurations for common developer experience (DX) optimization scenarios. See the provider routing guide for the full API reference on `sort`, `partition`, `preferred_max_latency`, and `preferred_min_throughput`.

### Recipe 1: Bounding Peak-Hour Queue Latency

Scenario: During peak global traffic hours (e.g. US morning rush), popular open-weight inference hosts can experience queue congestion, causing Time to First Token (TTFT) to spike. Solution: Use `preferred_max_latency` with a percentile cutoff (such as `p90`).

## Default Routing

For each model in your request, OpenRouter picks a provider by comparing what a good response would actually cost you at each one, not by list price alone. Each input is measured from recent production traffic, so routing reacts within minutes when a provider gets faster, slower, or less reliable:

- Effective price: the price the provider actually charges, reflecting its real cache hit rate and its typical mix of input and output tokens.
- Throughput: end-to-end output tokens per second. A faster provider can charge more and still win your request.
- Time to first token (TTFT): how long you wait before the response starts streaming.
- Rate limits: how often the provider rejects requests with a 429 because it is out of capacity.
- Reliability: how often requests fail because of the provider.
- Quality: whether the provider’s tool calls come back well formed.

Providers close to the best share most of the traffic, and each request picks one at random, weighted by those shares. Providers far behind still get a small share, so routing notices when they improve. On top of the shares:

- A provider whose errors or 429s are far worse than the model’s other providers gets no traffic until it recovers.
- Routing learns how much load each provider can take before it returns 429s, and sends the rest to other providers.
- A burst of 429s or a jump in latency briefly lowers a provider’s share.

If a request fails, the retry is picked the same way from the providers that are left. Follow-up requests in a conversation stay with the same provider while its prompt cache is warm. For more detail on each input, see How OpenRouter Routes Traffic Between Providers.

When you send a request with `tools` or `tool_choice`, OpenRouter makes a best effort to route to providers known to support tool use. Similarly, if you set `max_output_tokens` (or `max_tokens` on Chat Completions), then OpenRouter will only route to providers that support a response of that length.

Default routing applies whenever you leave the choice of provider to OpenRouter. It is bypassed when you set `sort` (or a default provider sort in your account settings), use the `:floor` or `:nitro` shortcuts, set `order`, or use your own provider key. If you set `only` or `ignore` and two or more providers remain, default routing picks among them.

## Provider Sorting

As described above, default routing balances price against throughput, latency, and reliability. If you instead want to explicitly prioritize a particular provider attribute, you can include the `sort` field in the `provider` preferences. Default routing is bypassed, and the router will try providers in that order. The three sort options are:

- `"price"`: prioritize lowest price
- `"throughput"`: prioritize highest throughput
- `"latency"`: prioritize lowest latency

### How Percentiles Work

OpenRouter tracks latency and throughput metrics for each model and provider using percentile statistics calculated over a rolling 5-minute window. The available percentiles are:

- p50 (median): 50% of requests perform better than this value
- p75: 75% of requests perform better than this value
- p90: 90% of requests perform better than this value
- p99: 99% of requests perform better than this value

Higher percentiles (like p90 or p99) give you more confidence about worst-case performance, while lower percentiles (like p50) reflect typical performance. For example, if a model and provider has a p90 latency of 2 seconds, that means 90% of requests complete in under 2 seconds. When you specify multiple percentile cutoffs, all specified cutoffs must be met for a model and provider to be in the preferred group. This allows you to set both typical and worst-case performance requirements.

### Speed

Speed is the main factor that trades off against price: a faster endpoint can cost more and still win traffic. It’s measured as output tokens per second, end to end, so it includes TTFT: the user waits for the whole response, from sending the request to the last token.

### TTFT

TTFT adds directly to your adjusted price, even though it already counts toward speed, because interactive use depends on it most. It’s the time to first token: how long users wait before your response starts streaming. In agentic sessions, a model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.
Source: How OpenRouter Routes Traffic Between Providers (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/providers/traffic-routing)

## What one try costs: price plus waiting

For each request, the router estimates how many input and output tokens it will use from the model’s recent traffic. That one estimate sets both parts of a try: the price you would pay and the time you would wait.

### Effective price

Effective price is the price that the provider would actually charge you, calculated from recent measured traffic. It reflects the provider’s real cache hit rate and the model’s average mix of input and output tokens, so it can differ a lot from the list price. This ensures that a provider can’t win traffic by hiding expensive cached or output tokens behind a low input price.

The router prices your request at each provider’s effective price, and prioritizes the cheapest options.

### Throughput

Throughput is what trades off against price: a faster provider can charge more and still win your request. It’s measured as output tokens per second end-to-end, so it includes the time to first token plus the time it takes the provider to stream the entire output response. The router adds that wait to the Routing Cost using a conversion rate set per model, based on what its providers typically charge and how fast they are.

### Time to first token

Time to first token (TTFT) is how long you would wait before the response started streaming. It adds to the Routing Cost on its own, even though it already counts toward throughput, because interactive use depends on it most. In an agent session, the model may make many tool calls in a row, and each one waits for a first token.

In order to measure the impact of the new routing algorithm, we had to go beyond a standard A/B test, because changes in routing behavior can’t easily be isolated from the control group. For example, if the new algorithm did a better job of routing traffic away from a struggling provider, the old algorithm’s requests to that provider would find more capacity available and get faster, skewing the results. Further compounding the difficulty is the enormous variability in request shape and volume patterns. A single whale user that spins up an automated flurry of high effort requests to a single provider can artificially inflate the metrics for that provider regardless of which algorithm we used to route their requests.
